### Hiding `ring_dedup`'s synchronous all-to-alls behind the shared expert: no gain

Commit: 3838b71 (local, on the `ring_dedup` base 91286fc) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 454847, 454872, 454943 (overlap + latency-hiding scheduler); 454865, 454945, 454949 (latency-hiding scheduler only); 454857, 454892 (baseline)

```bash
JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton \
  XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true \
  sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 \
  --compilation-cache-dir <fresh private dir> --batch-size 64 --attention gpu_pallas_triton_flash \
  --moe-impl ring_dedup --pooled-transport-capacity-factor 1.1 --remat-mode save_moe
```

| Variant (`save_moe`) | Step | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 1.589 s | 14.23% | 206.5 GiB |
| latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s (best 1.569) | 14.36% | 207.7 GiB |
| shared expert pinned under the transfers + latency-hiding scheduler | 1.575 s | 14.36% | 208.2 GiB |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **What was tried.** A `custom_vjp` around `ring_dedup`'s return `all_to_all` runs the shared-expert MLP between the transfer's start and its use. The backward does the same for the dy `all_to_all` and the shared-expert backward. Ordering is enforced with `optimization_barrier`. The shared expert moves into the backend (`moe_mlp(..., shared_expert=...)`). f32 CPU tests on 8 shards match `ring_dedup` plus a separately computed shared expert to 1e-5 in value and in every gradient.
- **The forward return was already hidden.** In the default schedule the forward return `all_to_all` is async and spans the shared-expert forward GEMMs (30 of 45 ms per profiled step run under it). The synchronous forward transfer is the dispatch. The backward dy `all_to_all` is synchronous.
- **Without the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers backfire.** XLA's default GPU schedule doesn't move all-to-all starts earlier, so it placed the shared GEMMs before the start and every large `all_to_all` became synchronous: 1.610 s vs 1.589 s (+1.3%).
- **With the latency-hiding scheduler the barriers work, but the time just moves.** Unhidden ms per profiled step with the scheduler, before → after pinning:

  | Transfer | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | dy | 41 | 26 |
  | dx | 7 | 33 |
  | forward return | 66 | 90 |

  The scheduler was already hiding dx behind the shared backward. It won't split that work across dy and dx, and scheduling-group annotations, which could force the split, crash the compiler on this ROCm build.
- **`recompute_all`:** baseline 1.707 s, scheduler only 1.695 s, scheduler + pinning 1.703 s.
- **The latency-hiding scheduler alone** gives -0.9% (`save_moe`) and -0.7% (`recompute_all`) here, but an earlier run measured +0.7%. That's within run-to-run noise (about 1.5%), so the defaults stay as they are.
- **Next:** profile-guided latency-hiding scheduling (`xla_gpu_pgle_profile_file_or_directory_path`), so the scheduler fills windows by measured transfer time; or find other independent work for the forward dispatch window.

</details>

| 2 nodes, EP8 + FSDP across nodes | 192 | 3.020 s | 260,373 | 11.22% | 77% | 165.5 GiB |

- Setup: the 14.31% configuration (flash attention, Triton `ragged_dot`, `ring_dedup` at transport capacity 1.1, `save_moe`) at 8 or 12 sequences per GPU. Step is the median of steps 2-19, with a fresh compile per run. MFU is against the peak of all GPUs in the run.

RCCL uses GPU Direct RDMA over them with default settings. rccl-tests on 16 GPUs reach 218 GB/s bus bandwidth for all-reduce, all-gather and reduce-scatter (366-392 GB/s on one node) and 89 GB/s for all-to-all (349 GB/s on one node). </details>

comments.body:
🤖 ### bf16 XLA grouped GEMM on MI350X: hipBLASLt has no bf16 grouped kernels for gfx950, and its one fp16 grouped kernel is 8-21x slower than Triton

Commit: none (standalone JAX script, no Marin code) · GPU: one MI350X per configuration, run side by side on one node · Job: 460950

```bash
# $WORK/marin/.venv: JAX 0.11.0, jax-rocm10-plugin, ROCm 10.0.0 from pip.
# Command buffers stay off because hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM crashes with them on (#9904).
# Times jax.lax.ragged_dot (fwd) and its VJP (bwd: dlhs and drhs) by wall clock over 20 calls,
# then sums GPU kernel time by kernel name over 5 calls under jax.profiler.
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype bfloat16  # bf16, XLA default
XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=" python gg_profile.py --dtype float16   # fp16, hipBLASLt grouped GEMM
```

Useful TFLOP/s per call (2·M·K·N per pass, counting only each row's own expert). Shapes are per GPU as in #9859 (w13: fused gate/up projection; w2: down projection), with 32 experts and equal row counts. bwd is dlhs and drhs together. The Triton column is #9859's tile-map kernels at the same shapes (job 457866, from the PR description); for bwd it gives the combined rate, then dlhs / drhs.

| Shape (M, K, N) | Pass | bf16 XLA (default) | fp16 XLA grouped GEMM | bf16 Triton, #9859 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13, batch 64 (131072, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 35.6 | 37.4 | 784 |
| | bwd | 29.5 | 38.9 | 743 (806 / 689) |
| June w2, batch 64 (131072, 1280, 2560) | fwd | 36.6 | 52.9 | 725 |
| | bwd | 27.1 | 38.1 | 696 (764 / 639) |
| June w13, batch 8 (16384, 2560, 2560) | fwd | 36.2 | 36.5 | 621 |
| | bwd | 33.5 | 71.3 | 562 (632 / 506) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- **Relaxing XLA's gate is not enough.** XLA lowers `ragged_dot` to hipBLASLt's grouped GEMM only where `CanBeHandledByGpublasltGroupGemm` in `xla/hlo/transforms/expanders/ragged_dot_rewriter.cc` allows it: fp16 and bf16 on gfx942, fp16 only on gfx950 (openxla/xla#38088, unchanged on XLA `main`). The gate follows hipBLASLt's kernel coverage. The gfx950 kernel libraries in hipBLASLt from ROCm 7.1 and 7.2 (the cluster's system installs) and ROCm 10.0 (pip) have grouped-GEMM kernels for fp16 only, and `ROCm/rocm-libraries` `develop` has no bf16 grouped-GEMM tuning logic for gfx950. A plugin rebuilt with the gate relaxed would have no bf16 kernel to call.
- **The gfx950 fp16 grouped GEMM has one kernel.** Each gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM logic file in [`rocm-libraries`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/tree/develop/projects/hipblaslt/library/src/amd_detail/rocblaslt/src/Tensile/Logic/asm_full/gfx950/gfx950/GridBased) (about 9 KB) lists a single solution with a 16x16x32 tile. The gfx942 bf16 grouped-GEMM files list 4-7 MB of tuned solutions per layout. In the profiles, that `MT16x16x32` kernel accounts for the whole fp16 call. bf16 and fp16 matrix-core throughput is the same on gfx950, so a bf16 build of the same kernel would not be faster. XLA's setup kernel (`SetUserArgsKernelRaggedIn*Dim`) takes about 6 µs per GEMM.
- **XLA's default bf16 path does 32x the useful work.** It runs one hipBLASLt matmul of every row against every expert's weights at 1.20-1.42 PFLOP/s, then masks the result. The matmul is 68-91% of the call, and transposes and the mask take the rest. fp16 with `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_grouped_gemm=false` takes the same path at 25-34 TFLOP/s.
- **The possible gain is small.** On MI300X, where hipBLASLt has tuned bf16 grouped kernels, XLA's grouped GEMM took 11-28% less time per call than tuned Triton (#9904, microbenchmarks only). Triton `ragged_dot` was 21% of the MI350X batch-64 step in [this profile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123445), taken before the kernel rewrite and flash attention. If the MI300X edge carried over to gfx950, it would save about 2-6% of step time (21% × 11-28%), and less now that the rewritten Triton kernels are faster.
- **If someone picks this up:** test fp16 first, because it needs no plugin rebuild. Generate large-tile gfx950 fp16 grouped-GEMM solutions from the `rocm-libraries` tag that matches ROCm 10.0.0, and set `HIPBLASLT_TENSILE_LIBPATH` to a copy of the stock gfx950 library directory with the new files added. Add bf16 solutions and rebuild the plugin with the gate relaxed only if fp16 beats Triton. The other route is to ask AMD to ship tuned gfx950 grouped-GEMM kernels in hipBLASLt. Until then, MI350X keeps Triton `ragged_dot`.

</details>

issues.body:
A single plain `DaytonaError` causes a Harbor eval record to be marked `infra_failed` with empty `metrics`. Harbor's error taxonomy (`harbor_config/errors.py`) lists `DaytonaProcessError`, `DaytonaDockerSetupError`, and `DaytonaSandboxStopError`, but omits the base `DaytonaError` raised by the Daytona SDK when session creation fails. The runner records the trial as `unknown:DaytonaError`, so `_evaluation_outcome` (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py`) rejects the whole run as taxonomy drift.

The affected TBLite-100 run used Harbor 38742b0f. Its [record](s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-233725-v7-plain-low-v01-20261020-openthoughts-tblite-100-66da/record.json) reports `EvaluationError: Harbor eval encountered error names absent from its taxonomy under '…/results': unknown:DaytonaError=1`. Trial `harbor_openthoughts-tblite_8b8e96c3cc54/cpp-daemon-sighup-segfault__2uaQ4iL/attempts/000` has `exception_type: DaytonaError` and message `Failed to create session:` with empty detail. The same run's `results/harbor_result.json` already contains a complete aggregate: 100 attempted, 93 scored, 12 solved, mean reward 0.146, and errors `AgentTimeoutError 42, ModelInitiatedTmuxFailure 4, TmuxBatchProtocolError 3, TmuxSessionEndedError 2, TmuxCommandError 1, unknown:DaytonaError 1`.

About 2 h of an 8×H100 serve produced a usable score that the record discards. The same error can affect any Daytona-backed Harbor eval.

A session-create failure should count as an infrastructure error because the model never ran. For this run, the record should report 12 solved of 93 scored, mean reward 0.146, and completion 93/100 = 0.93, above the default 0.9 gate (`DEFAULT_MIN_COMPLETION_RATE`). It should list these seven unscored trials and their error types:

| Task | Error |
|---|---|
| basic-message-queue | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| grid-pathfinding | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| iot-device-registration-server | TmuxBatchProtocolError |
| maven-slf4j-conflict | TmuxSessionEndedError |
| sign-vector-game | TmuxSessionEndedError |
| image-tile-identification | TmuxCommandError |
| cpp-daemon-sighup-segfault | DaytonaError |

Classify `DaytonaError` as `ErrorCategory.INFRASTRUCTURE` in `src/harbor_config/errors.py` in marin-community/harbor (missing at 38742b0f and on main), then bump the Harbor pin. The drift check works as designed; the missing name causes the rejection.

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
## Summary

A Harbor eval record is marked `infra_failed`, and its `metrics` are empty, when a single trial raises a plain `DaytonaError`. Harbor's error taxonomy (`harbor_config/errors.py`) lists `DaytonaProcessError`, `DaytonaDockerSetupError` and `DaytonaSandboxStopError`, but not the base `DaytonaError`. The base class is what the Daytona SDK raises for a failed session create. The runner records the trial as `unknown:DaytonaError`, and `_evaluation_outcome` (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/runner.py`) rejects the whole run as taxonomy drift.

## Example

- Record: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261020-233725-v7-plain-low-v01-20261020-openthoughts-tblite-100-66da/record.json` (TBLite-100, Harbor 38742b0f)
- Record error: `EvaluationError: Harbor eval encountered error names absent from its taxonomy under '…/results': unknown:DaytonaError=1`
```

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Resuming from a committed epoch checkpoint into a root containing later uncommitted checkpoints can fail on the next save. A 32-H100 Snowball SFT continuation restored step 320, completed the remaining 642 updates, then failed while finalizing an asynchronous save into the existing step-641 directory:

```text
ValueError: FAILED_PRECONDITION: Error opening "zarr3" driver:
Expected "chunk_shape" of [2560] but received: [80]
array: model/transformer/blocks/1/rms_attn/weight
checkpoint: checkpoints/step-641/
```

The checkpoint barrier subsequently timed out after 30 minutes, and the gang exited before producing its final HF export.

Reproduce:
1. Train with permanent epoch checkpoints at zero-based steps 320, 641 and 962. Interrupt the run while later checkpoint writes are incomplete, leaving `step-320/metadata.json` committed, a step-641 TensorStore payload without `metadata.json`, and a manifest-only step-962 directory.
2. Resume from the committed step-320 checkpoint with the same output root. Keep the incomplete later directories in place.
3. Continue through the remaining epoch boundaries. In the observed continuation, the save requested chunk shape `[2560]` for an array whose partial write stored `[80]`. TensorStore raised the error above; the asynchronous failure surfaced at the terminal checkpoint hook, after training had completed. The reason the requested chunk shape changed after restore has not yet been isolated, so this is an observed reproduction rather than a reduced deterministic test.

Observed on `cw-rno2a`, 2026-10-21, with four eight-H100 tasks, batch 16 × 32,768, eight-way expert parallelism, four-way context parallelism, and native checkpoints every 321 updates. Both the original run and continuation used `11d41241ec`, `experiments/post_training/agentic_sweep/arms.py`, and `--parent v0.1 --arm relay --data-variant low --learning-rate 1e-6 --epochs 3 --hf-export-schedule final-only`. No mesh or optimizer change was requested on resume. The original coordinator `/karan/arm-train-relay-low-v0p1-v7-20261021-cw-rno2a` was killed at 18:47 UTC during the controller outage in #10433. Its root retained a committed step 320 (16:48 UTC), an uncommitted step-641 payload (17:49–17:54 UTC), and a manifest-only step 962 (18:30 UTC).

Continuation `/karan/arm-train-relay-low-v0p1-v7-20261021-cw-rno2a-r3`, at `11d41241ec`, selected step 320 at 19:20 UTC. It reached step 641 at 20:09 UTC and the last optimizer update, step 962, at 20:41 UTC. At 21:11 UTC the terminal hook surfaced the step-641 chunk-layout error and checkpoint barrier timeout. Fresh object reads found neither a step-641 nor a step-962 commit marker. The original partial directories are preserved under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/checkpoints/karan/relay-low-v0.1-v7-20261021-lr1e-06-3ep/2026.10.21/checkpoints/`.

Two plain SFT runs using the same batch size and mesh committed their epoch saves in clean roots; those runs exported HF after epoch 2 and at the final step. A third plain SFT run using final-only HF exports also committed its first epoch, step 205, in a clean root. These observations show that final-only HF exports alone do not prevent native saves; they do not isolate every condition needed for the chunk-layout mismatch.

Expected: On resume, identify later step directories lacking a commit marker and remove or version those incomplete writes before reusing their step numbers. A terminal checkpoint write should start in an empty directory when a stale incomplete directory exists, without reopening its incompatible arrays. Preserve committed checkpoints, and report asynchronous save failures before allowing an entire additional epoch to run.

Related: #9380 reports a chunk-layout mismatch when rewriting an already committed final checkpoint after a resume with no new optimizer updates. This case concerns uncommitted later checkpoints encountered while continuing from an earlier committed epoch. Part of #10213.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Checkpoint discovery requires `metadata.json`, so the continuation correctly restored step 320 while leaving the uncommitted step 641 payload in place. `Checkpointer` then reused the fixed `step-641` destination; TensorStore opened arrays already carrying a different chunk grid. The previous asynchronous save is checked at the next save or during trainer exit, which can delay the error until another epoch has run.

**Relevant code**
- [`checkpoint.py#L638-L667`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e524e9e12773de7be3f1e7fd8fc80c8d356ef275/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L638-L667) — fixed step destination
- [`checkpoint.py#L840-L915`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e524e9e12773de7be3f1e7fd8fc80c8d356ef275/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L840-L915) — completion marker follows writes
- [`checkpoint.py#L1217-L1243`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e524e9e12773de7be3f1e7fd8fc80c8d356ef275/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L1217-L1243) — committed-directory discovery
- [`tensorstore_serialization.py#L678-L820`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e524e9e12773de7be3f1e7fd8fc80c8d356ef275/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tensorstore_serialization.py#L678-L820) — prior-save wait and array open
- [`trainer.py#L412-L430`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e524e9e12773de7be3f1e7fd8fc80c8d356ef275/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L412-L430) — final asynchronous wait

# Proposed Fix

Give each save invocation a fresh checkpoint directory, such as `step-641-<save-id>`, with one ID chosen on process 0 and shared across the gang. Keep `metadata.json` as the completion marker and numeric step as its source of truth. Existing `step-N` checkpoints remain readable; a resumed save never reopens a prior attempt's arrays, including an uncommitted attempt or a committed final-step save (#9380). This avoids deleting an old writer's payload while it may still be active.

Audit readers and operational scripts that assume an exact `step-N` directory name. Discovery already reads the step from metadata, but direct path construction may need updating. Add a nonblocking check of completed asynchronous saves to each training checkpoint hook and before final hooks/export. Raise the original failure as soon as the background commit finishes while preserving asynchronous training when it is still running.

Test with local TensorStore data: leave a step 641 payload with incompatible chunk metadata and no commit marker, restore step 320, save step 641, and verify that the new checkpoint loads while the old payload and committed step 320 are untouched. Cover a repeated committed final step, cross-process agreement on the save path, and a real failed asynchronous write reported before the next scheduled save. Keep orphan cleanup separate from the save path; it needs an age threshold and an inactive-writer check before deleting object-store data.

The path change reaches checkpoint producers, direct-path consumers, and asynchronous trainer error handling, so this needs a design and regression pass rather than a one-line overwrite fix. No open PR matched #10453 or the chunk-layout failure. The remaining decision is the retention window for abandoned attempt directories; it does not block save isolation.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |

| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

| Reversed launch-order timing | Bound short-run timing variation | [Preferred W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-speed-rep-step126k-01a0c066-a1), [current W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-speed-rep-step126k-01a0c066-a1) |
| Corrected current-checkpoint Paloma | Evaluate the complete learned state under current arithmetic | `/romain/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2`; [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-current-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) |
| Corrected preferred-checkpoint Paloma | Same fixed policy and pending query-bias handling | `/romain/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-coord-01a0c066-a2`; [W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-router-pref-fixed-eval-qb-step126020-01a0c066-a2) |

Both continuation jobs and both corrected Paloma jobs completed all 16 tasks without failures or preemptions.

The earlier fixed-evaluation `a1` runs omitted each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. They are superseded by the corrected `a2` runs above. The separate evaluation-path problem is tracked in [#9352](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9352).

### Saved-input accuracy

The fixture contains 324 valid layer-15 entries representing 32 byte-distinct activation vectors. The production-shape probe tiles the entries to 65,536 rows and preserves their captured frequency.

| Arithmetic | Score RMS error | Maximum error | Top-8 order versus FP64 reference | Isolated forward | Isolated backward |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current BF16 output, then FP32 cast | `0.0074565` | `0.0311123` | 80/324 entries changed | 14.07 ms | 14.43 ms |
| BF16 operands, FP32 accumulation/output | `0.00002808` | `0.00007003` | all 324 matched | 14.07 ms | 14.48 ms |
| FP32 operands | `0.00000416` | `0.00002373` | all 324 matched | 18.20 ms | 23.26 ms |

The isolated timing covers only the saved-input router dot and gradient. It is not a whole-step measurement.

### Continuation measurements

| Post-compile metric, 19 real batches | Current | Preferred FP32 accumulation | Preferred minus current |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Median train throughput | 275,523 tok/s | 271,399 tok/s | -1.50% by ratio of medians |
| Median full iteration | 16.3871 s | 16.5275 s | +0.86% by ratio of medians |
| Final cumulative peak HBM | 115.5375 GiB | 115.5375 GiB | 0 |
| Mean train loss | 1.24572355 | 1.24572228 | -0.00000127 |
| Mean sender drops | 684,900 | 722,882 | +37,983 (+5.55%) |
| Mean routing entropy | 5.945189 | 5.945129 | -0.000060 |
| Mean expert-count CV | 0.097451 | 0.098131 | +0.000680 |

The corrected Paloma macro losses were `2.22016478` for the current continuation and `2.22088742` for the preferred continuation. The runs used current router arithmetic for both checkpoints and applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias state. This common policy removes evaluation-time router rounding as a direct difference. It also evaluates the preferred-trained checkpoint under arithmetic different from its training policy, so the sign is not a clean estimate of long-run preferred-policy quality.

comments.author: mindscanlabs
comments.body:
**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. So a 4K-era forecast scored against the 16K final value, as in H1 and H4 of the forecast linked above, starts about 0.03 high from the packing change alone. The offset may also drift over the remaining 16K training, so if it's cheap, one 4K eval of the final checkpoint would let these forecasts be checked at the 4K packing they were built on. issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
tl;dr

PivotRL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) is a flavor of RL that was used extensively in Nemotron-Ultra post-training. It operates on existing SFT trajectories to combine the compute efficiency of SFT with the OOD accuracy of E2E RL. PivotRL first executes local, on-policy rollouts and filters for pivots: informative intermediate turns where sampled actions exhibit high variance in outcomes; then it utilizes rewards for functional-equivalent actions rather than demanding strict string matching with the SFT data demonstration.

MarinSkyRL training data resolves to two kinds, a plain directory (`ArtifactDataSource`) and a TaskTrove parquet cohort (`TaskTroveDataSource`). Neither carries per-step annotations.

Scope: a Marin data source that resolves per-step pivot annotations with artifact identity, request plumbing for them, and a `MARIN_SKYRL` pin bump (`lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:73`) to a MarinSkyRL revision that consumes the annotations and applies step weights in the training loop.

Open questions:

- Compute pivot scores (teacher-forced NLL under the student) as a Marin
  artifact step, or accept only precomputed annotations?
- Carry detection parameters (spike threshold, pivot weight) as named
  `SkyRLSpec` fields or leave them to `config_yaml` and `overrides`?

Done when:

- A pivot-annotated source resolves to a `ResolvedDataSource` whose
  identity covers the annotations, so the step fingerprint changes when
  annotations change.
- `SkyRLLaunchRequest` carries the annotations, and the pinned MarinSkyRL
  commit applies non-uniform step weights end to end.
- Annotation-free specs keep today's fingerprints and training behavior.
- `tests/rl/test_skyrl.py` covers the new source kind and request fields.
- We can reproduce this result from the paper E2E in MarinSkyRL -> 'On GSM8K (200 problems, 182 Kimi K2.5 competition-math traces, Gemma 4 E4B student), pivot-weighted SFT at 2.5x loss scored 80.0% vs 74.5% for uniform SFT against an 85.5% base."

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Two released NVIDIA datasets are good candidate targets for the first Snowball PivotRL experiment:

- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1), pinned at `4947a3c8ea803413a65f9eca14a96ef521b2ddf5`. The current release has 50,308 pivot rows with `trajectory_id`, prefix position, `expected_action`, and profiling counts/pass rate (`pass_rate_total` is 8 in the inspected rows).
- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1), pinned at `eaef26944643644c8a3dbbf361ce6128142f5976`. It has 31,111 pivot rows with `expected_answer`, `source_trajectory_uid`, and `pivot_agent_turn_index` from GLM-5.1/Terminus-2 trajectories.

These releases correct the assumption in the issue that no training data is public. They are sufficient for a method-level reproduction, but not an exact reproduction of the paper: the SWE release is not the paper's reported 87,718-example filtered set, and the Terminal release uses a later teacher/task mixture.

Prepare separate SWE and Terminal artifacts first. Split SWE by `trajectory_id` and Terminal by `metadata.source_trajectory_uid`, not by row, so neighboring prefixes from one trajectory cannot cross train/validation. The adapter should map `responses_create_params.input` to `prompt`, preserve tools and request options, carry the expected action/answer and source identity in `extra_info`, and emit a single-turn local functional-verifier environment. SWE can reuse the existing `nemotron_ultra` action comparator after normalizing the released agent name; Terminal needs an `expected_answer` verifier case. The raw Hugging Face rows are not yet SkyRL-shaped and should not be passed directly to `PromptDataset`.

For iteration, use the two Harbor evals already implemented in Marin:

- SWE-bench Verified random-100: `swebench`
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: `tb2`

Both are in-distribution for this experiment and are safe to inspect and hill climb. Keep the policy's OOD suite untouched until the checkpoint and hyperparameters are frozen. The current launcher command is:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model <registered-snowball-pivot-checkpoint> \
  --evals swebench,tb2 \
  --priority interactive \
  --no-wait
```

The checked-in Harbor policies use Terminus-2 + Daytona; `swebench` points at the fixed random-100 set and `tb2` points at Marin's Terminal-Bench 2 dataset. This also gives us a direct comparison with the Snowball R2E-Gym result in #9225.

Proposed training overlay below. Apply it to `cloud/iris/configs/snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml` so the tested Megatron/vLLM placement and model geometry remain unchanged. `<...>` values are immutable prepared artifacts produced from one of the pinned releases above. Run SWE and Terminal as separate primary arms; a balanced mixture is a follow-up experiment.

```yaml
# snowball_pivotrl_split64.yaml: overlay on snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml
entrypoint: standard

context_budget:
  request_window_tokens: 65536
  max_turns: 1
  max_new_tokens_per_turn: null  # proposed: use all context remaining after this row's prefix

trainer:
  strategy: megatron
  seed: 42
  algorithm:
    advantage_estimator: grpo
    grpo_norm_by_std: true
    advantage_batch_normalize: false
    eps_clip_low: 0.2
    eps_clip_high: 0.2
    use_entropy_loss: false
    use_kl_in_reward: false
    use_kl_loss: true
    kl_loss_coef: 0.001
    loss_reduction: token_mean
    dynamic_sampling:
      type: null                 # frozen released pivots: closest paper-like arm
      max_sample_batches: 30
      min_replace_ratio: 0.3
      informative_on: unshaped
      min_reward_std: 0.0
  epochs: 1
  max_steps: 130                # paper's disclosed SWE run length
  update_epochs_per_batch: 1
  train_batch_size: 64          # 64 unique pivot prefixes
  policy_mini_batch_size: 1024  # 64 prefixes x 16 responses
  eval_batch_size: 100
  micro_forward_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  use_sample_packing: true
  eval_before_train: true
  eval_interval: 10
  ckpt_interval: 10
  max_ckpts_to_keep: 3
  resume_mode: none
  logger: wandb
  project_name: snowball-pivotrl
  # Keep policy/ref Megatron configs and split64 placement unchanged.

generator:
  backend: vllm
  n_samples_per_prompt: 16
  eval_n_samples_per_prompt: 1
  sampling_params:
    temperature: 1.0
    top_p: 1.0
    top_k: -1
  # Keep the tested split64 engine topology and Hermes tool parser unchanged.

data:
  kind: parquet
  train_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/train.parquet>
  val_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/validation.parquet>
  shuffle: true
```

The prepared rows should use `env_class: nemotron_ultra`; retain the existing `environment.skyrl_gym.nemotron_ultra` block. Each pivot rollout must terminate after one sampled action and use the local functional verifier.

`max_new_tokens_per_turn: null` is proposed syntax, not accepted by the current launcher. For a single-turn pivot there should be no separate generation budget: set each request's `max_tokens` to `request_window_tokens - tokenized_prefix_length` and let the model use the remaining context. `ContextBudget` currently requires a positive fixed output allowance and subtracts it from every row's prompt allowance; #9176 should make that field nullable for `max_turns: 1` (or add an equivalent remaining-context mode). Reusing the end-to-end RLVR config's 6,528-token cap would truncate valid pivot actions for no methodological reason.

The `64 x 16` geometry yields 1,024 rollout trajectories per trainer step. Confirm that count in the first rollout manifest before a full run. Start with a bounded startup/memory smoke, then run the static arm above. A Marin-specific follow-up can set `dynamic_sampling.type: filter` with `informative_on: unshaped` to replace stale all-pass/all-fail groups online; that is useful, but it is no longer the paper's frozen-pivot method.

The paper does not disclose the KL coefficient. Pre-register `0`, `0.001`, and `0.01` and report all three instead of selecting one retrospectively from SWE-bench/TB2.1. Keep reward shaping disabled so group informativeness is computed from the binary functional outcome.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Add support for Harbor's host-side Claude Code adapter in the shared task rollout path. The controller should run on the host while its task tools operate in the sandbox.

Current main (`2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950`) routes task rollouts through RolloutEngine. Its [agent adapter](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/2b08e2432c8871b7e6c4cd7c389d7bb2df2b4950/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py) requires `BaseInstalledAgent` and rejects host-side Harbor agents. Host-side means the controller runs in the rollout-worker process or a host subprocess while task commands execute in a sandbox. Harbor already provides [ClaudeCodeLocal](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/aee476676983dfa62f5d824538193302ef46e3f9/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py), selected by `name: claude-code` and `mode: local`. It derives from `BaseAgent` and is rejected by the current adapter.

Done when:

- Document and validate the local-mode configuration, client version, supported model endpoint, and sandbox tool routing. Reuse Harbor's adapter and establish which operations remain on the host.
- Demonstrate whether the client can use the trainable policy through the supported protocol bridge. For on-policy RL, retain exact served tokens and behavior log probabilities and verify their alignment with training inputs.
- Reject unsupported client/backend/objective combinations before allocating a full run. A fixed external Claude model used to collect teacher trajectories must be labeled separately; it is not an on-policy rollout of the trainable model.
- Test concurrent-trial isolation, credential boundaries, timeout and error classification, cancellation, verifier execution, and cleanup of host processes and containers.
- For a supported trainable-policy configuration, complete a live multi-turn smoke through verification, an optimizer update, and synchronized evaluation. Preserve reproducible configs and traces, exclude credentials, and review client-supplied instructions before publication.

Endpoint compatibility and training-evidence support require validation; this request does not assert that selecting local mode alone makes Claude Code usable for on-policy RL. If the client cannot support the required trainable-policy endpoint, record that blocker with evidence; teacher-only collection does not complete this integration request.


Transferred from https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10385.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Open design question shared by marin-community/marin#10387, marin-community/marin#10386, and marin-community/marin#10385: can the agent implementations remain in Harbor, with MarinSkyRL collecting the training evidence through an adapter? Is there a concrete operational constraint that requires porting them into Marin?

Please compare two ownership models before choosing an implementation:

- Harbor owns the full trial: agent controller, environment lifecycle, retries, and verification. MarinSkyRL supplies policy inference and captures training evidence.
- RolloutEngine owns the trial: its adapter runs Harbor's agent controller and propagates cancellation to it, while Marin manages environment lifecycle and verification.

For either option, establish how the integration retains exact model requests, sampled tokens, behavior log probabilities, tool observations, and verifier outcomes. Assign explicit owners for inference-request retries, tool-operation retries, whole-trial retries, cancellation, and cleanup, without duplicate handling of the same operation. Preserve original Harbor errors and diagnostics when mapping outcomes to MarinSkyRL's training decisions: include, exclude, or fail.

Keeping the implementations and, where practical, the full trial lifecycle in Harbor may avoid duplicating its operational behavior. This remains an architectural question, not a decided requirement or a claim that the current adapter supports it. What would prevent that arrangement, and what tests would establish that Marin's tracking and training interfaces can observe it correctly?

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Current MarinSkyRL has a Harbor-owned full-trial path for setup, verification, and cleanup, but its training runner requires `BaseInstalledAgent`; Harbor's `ClaudeCodeLocal` derives from `BaseAgent` and cannot enter it. Harbor exposes an Anthropic Messages translation route, while the local adapter inherits the host environment and launches a host subprocess; the reviewed code does not establish trainable-policy routing, per-trial request correlation, or cleanup of that subprocess on cancellation. Marin pins separate Harbor and MarinSkyRL revisions, so a validated integration must update those pins and its reproducible run config.

**Relevant code**
- [MarinSkyRL `agent_runtime.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py#L150-L213) — Harbor-owned trial path.
- [MarinSkyRL `harbor_trial_session.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/82396a73a31e776229f3240c3af2b50ad53c4336/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/harbor_trial_session.py#L49-L64) — installed-agent gate and session correlation.
- [Harbor `claude_code.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/agents/local/claude_code.py#L97-L222) — host CLI, inherited environment, cleanup.
- [Harbor `native_routes.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/e96b6dcca1513e97e43523eaa971a85c68fcedae/src/harbor/literal/native_routes.py#L173-L217) — Messages and token-count routes.
- [Marin `external_dependencies.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L64-L79) — runtime pins.

# Design

Use the existing Harbor-owned full-trial path. Harbor owns the agent process, sandbox, verifier, whole-trial retry, and cleanup; MarinSkyRL owns policy inference, exact model-turn evidence, and training inclusion decisions. The RolloutEngine-owned borrowed-machine path would require duplicating Harbor's environment and verifier lifecycle. This choice can be shared with the related host-agent requests in #10386 and #10387. No open PR for this adapter was found in the Marin or MarinSkyRL searches.

## Challenges

The Claude CLI must speak the bridge's supported Messages protocol and route every policy request through it. A successful Harbor trial alone cannot establish that the recorded tokens, log probabilities, and training masks match the policy's actual turns.

## Costs / Risks

The rollout worker would need a pinned host CLI. Host credentials, CLI session files, and task-supplied instructions require explicit isolation and review before traces are published.

## Implementation

1. **Prove the protocol first.** Pin a Claude Code CLI version and run its local mode against Harbor's `/v1/messages` and `/v1/messages/count_tokens` bridge with a trainable-policy server. Check model naming, streaming, tool calls, compaction, and that every model request reaches that server. Compare the server's exact prompt/completion token IDs and behavior log probabilities with the recorded turns and training projection, including masks after tool observations. If any required endpoint or evidence is unavailable, reject on-policy configuration before a full run and record the failing request and trace. Label fixed external-model collection as teacher data.
2. **Wire only a proven configuration.** Give each local trial an explicit model endpoint, model name, and scoped capability credential. Correlate its requests at its dedicated proxy, since the CLI does not currently provide the installed-agent correlation header. Admit `ClaudeCodeLocal` to the Harbor-owned trial path while keeping the borrowed-machine path restricted to installed agents. Validate the client version, backend, objective, and supported request modes at launch.
3. **Close lifecycle and credential gaps.** Pass the host process only the required runtime variables and trial-scoped credentials; keep task tools inside the sandbox. On timeout or cancellation, terminate and reap the CLI process, then close the proxy and Harbor environment. Preserve Harbor's original error and verifier details when choosing include, exclude, or fail. Bound client and bridge inference-request retries; let Harbor own whole-trial retries, with no second retry of the same trial in RolloutEngine.

## Testing

Exercise two concurrent trials, tool routing, credential separation, endpoint failure, timeout, cancellation, verifier execution, retry classification, and cleanup. Then run a bounded multi-turn Daytona smoke through verification, a non-skipped optimizer update, and evaluation after weight synchronization. Save exact pins, config, token/log-probability alignment checks, and sanitized traces; review client-supplied instructions before publication. Update Marin's pins and documentation only after the protocol and smoke gates pass.

## Open Questions

Can a pinned Claude Code CLI use the Messages bridge without changing model-visible requests or losing the evidence required for the chosen RL objective? This decides whether on-policy support is feasible; local mode alone does not.

Marin promotes an all-ungraded sample summary only when an aggregate graded count equals the attempted count; `task_item_count()` currently ignores `scored_count`. The pinned CRUXEval adapter writes `input_pass@1` and `output_pass@1` but no aggregate count, although its per-direction pass-rate maps identify the graded task IDs. - [`runner.py#L154-L179`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4aa26ec73d248b974766f8940a896a8c888d8269/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L154-L179) — count reconciliation

# Proposed Fix
